The investigation was conducted on a production turbojet engine with an axial-flow compressor pressure ratio of approximately 7.
Rotating stall patterns with 4, 5, and 6 stall zones were detected in the compressor.
The stall frequency relative to the rotor was approximately proportional to engine speed.
The fundamental bending frequencies of the first-stage rotor blades ranged from 163-178 Hz.
The highest vibratory stress measured was +34,800 lb/sq in at around 70% of rated engine speed.
Vibration bursts lasted from 10 to 350 cycles, with longer bursts corresponding to higher vibratory stresses.
Good correlation was found between the 5-zone stall frequency relative to the rotor and the blade vibration frequency at 65-72% of rated speed.
Reducing the guide vane turning or jet nozzle area caused the stall patterns to persist to higher speeds, up to 73% of rated speed.
The reduced guide vane turning increased the radial extent of the stall in the first-stage stator and decreased the amplitude of the flow fluctuations in the third stage.
The investigation was terminated by a fatigue failure of a first-stage rotor blade due to the high vibratory stresses.
Blades with magnets installed had lower natural bending frequencies than the standard blades.
The magneted blade reached its maximum vibratory stress at a lower engine speed than the standard blades.
Stall patterns with 6 zones were not detected with the standard guide vanes and jet nozzle configurations.
The duration of the vibration bursts corresponded to the time that the 5-zone and 6-zone stall patterns were present in the compressor.
The amplitude of the flow fluctuations due to rotating stall varied considerably with time, and were difficult to identify below 50% of design speed.
